posts.title: Where Blush Actually Belongs on a Rounder Face (Hint: Not Just the Apples)
posts.excerpt: Blush placement can make or break your face shape. If you have a rounder face, the classic 'smile and apply to the apples' advice might be widening your cheeks. Here's how to place blush so it lifts and defines, plus daylight checks and mistakes to avoid.
content: Why the Apples of Your Cheeks Might Be Working Against You

You've heard it a thousand times: smile big, find the roundest part of your cheek, and swirl on blush. It's the default advice, and for some face shapes, it works fine. But if your face is on the rounder side, that technique can backfire. Here's why: when you smile, your cheek muscles push up and out, creating a temporary fullness. Applying blush right on that spot emphasizes that fullness even when you stop smiling. The result? Your cheeks look wider, not lifted.

Think about it this way. Round faces have soft curves and a width that's roughly equal to their length. The goal with blush isn't to add more roundness. It's to create a subtle diagonal that draws the eye upward and inward, mimicking the effect of a gentle lift. That means moving your blush placement slightly higher and more toward the outer corner of your cheek, rather than the center of the apple.

I learned this the hard way after years of wondering why my blush always made my face look a little puffier than I wanted. Once I shifted the placement up and out, the difference was immediate. My cheeks looked more defined, and my whole face seemed more awake. So let's break down exactly where to put that blush.
Find Your Blush Sweet Spot: The Diagonal Lift

The key to lifting a round face with blush is to follow the natural diagonal line that runs from the apple of your cheek up toward your temple. Instead of concentrating the color on the apple itself, you'll start slightly higher and blend outward and upward. This creates a visual line that lifts the cheekbone and slims the face.

Here's how to find your starting point: look straight ahead in a mirror. Place two fingers on your cheekbone, right below the outer corner of your eye. That's roughly where your blush should begin. From there, sweep the color up and out toward your hairline, stopping just before you reach the edge of your face. The color should be most intense at the starting point and fade as it moves outward.

Avoid bringing the blush too close to your nose or too low on your cheek. Both of those placements can make your face look wider and rounder. Keep the focus on the outer half of your cheek for that lifted effect.
The Daylight Check: Why Indoor Lighting Lies

You've probably done your makeup in bathroom lighting that made everything look flawless, only to step outside and realize your blush is way too heavy or in the wrong spot. Indoor lighting, especially warm or dim lighting, can distort colors and shadows. That's why a daylight check is non-negotiable, especially when you're trying a new placement.

After you apply your blush, take a hand mirror and walk over to a window. Look at your face in natural light. You should see a soft, diffused wash of color that follows the diagonal line we talked about. If the blush looks like a bright stripe or sits too low on your cheek, adjust it before you leave the house. A quick blend with a clean brush or a damp sponge can fix most issues.

I also recommend checking from different angles. Turn your head slightly to the left and right. The blush should look balanced from all sides. If it's only visible from straight on, you might need to blend it a bit further out.
Common Mistakes That Widen a Round Face
Even with the right placement, a few habits can sabotage your efforts. Let's go through the most common ones I see, so you can avoid them.

First, applying too much color. A round face can handle blush, but a heavy hand can make the cheeks look like they're competing for attention. Start with a light layer and build up. It's easier to add than to take away.

Second, using the wrong brush. A large, fluffy brush can deposit color over a wide area, which can widen the face. Instead, use a smaller, angled brush to target the color precisely along the diagonal. Then blend with a clean, fluffy brush if needed.

Third, ignoring your undertone. Blush that clashes with your skin tone can look harsh and draw attention to the wrong areas. Choose shades that complement your complexion: peach and coral for warm undertones, pink and berry for cool undertones, and soft rose for neutral.
Fourth, placing blush too close to the nose. This can make the face look shorter and wider. Keep the inner edge of your blush aligned with the outer corner of your eye, or slightly beyond.
Finally, not blending enough. Harsh edges can look unnatural and emphasize the shape you're trying to soften. Take the time to blend, blend, blend.
Choosing the Right Blush Formula for a Lifted Look

The formula you choose can also affect how your blush wears and how easy it is to place. Powder blushes are classic and easy to blend, but they can look heavy if you're not careful. Cream blushes melt into the skin and give a natural, dewy finish, but they can be tricky to blend on top of foundation. Liquid and gel blushes are lightweight and sheer, but they dry quickly, so you need to work fast.

For a round face, I often recommend a cream or liquid blush because they blend seamlessly and can be layered without looking cakey. They also tend to look more natural, which helps with the lifting effect. If you prefer powder, choose a finely milled formula that blends easily and doesn't sit on top of the skin.

Application matters too. With cream or liquid, dot the product along the diagonal line and blend with your fingers or a damp sponge. With powder, tap off the excess and use a light hand, building in thin layers.
Step-by-Step: Blush Placement for a Round Face
Let's put it all together into a simple routine. Follow these steps for a lifted, flattering blush application every time.
1. Start with a clean, moisturized face. Apply your foundation and concealer as usual, and set with a light dusting of powder if you have oily skin.
2. Smile gently to find the apples of your cheeks, but don't apply blush there. Instead, use that as a reference point to find the diagonal line that runs from the apple up to your temple.
3. Load your brush or fingertips with a small amount of blush. Tap off any excess.
4. Starting at the outer corner of your eye, just below the brow bone, apply the blush in a sweeping motion toward your temple. Use light, feathery strokes.
5. Blend the edges with a clean brush or sponge to soften the color. Make sure there are no harsh lines.
6. Check your work in natural daylight. Adjust if needed by adding more color or blending further.
7. Finish with a setting spray if desired.
Blush and Contour: Friends or Foes?

Contour can be a great tool for defining a round face, but it can also compete with your blush if you're not careful. The key is to keep them in harmony. Contour should go in the hollows of your cheeks, while blush goes on the cheekbones. If you apply contour too close to your blush, the two can blend into a muddy mess.

A good rule of thumb: apply contour first, then blush. That way, you can see where the contour sits and place your blush slightly above it, following the diagonal line. This creates a layered effect that enhances the lift without looking overdone.
If you're not a contour person, that's fine too. Blush alone can do a lot for a round face when placed correctly. You don't need to contour every day to see a difference.
Quick Fixes for Blush Emergencies
We've all been there: you apply blush, step into daylight, and realize it's way too much or in the wrong spot. Don't panic. Here are some quick fixes.

If your blush is too heavy, take a clean, fluffy brush and gently sweep it over the area to diffuse the color. You can also use a damp sponge to press over the blush, which will lift some of the pigment.
If your blush is too low, use a concealer or foundation to cover the lower part and reapply higher up. Blend well.
If your blush looks patchy, blend it out with a clean brush or sponge. Sometimes adding a tiny bit of moisturizer or setting spray can help melt the product into the skin.
Prevention is better than cure, so always start with a light hand and build up. And remember that daylight check!
Final Thoughts: Trust the Process

Changing your blush placement can feel strange at first, especially if you've been doing the same thing for years. But give it a few tries. Practice on a day when you're not rushing, and check your reflection in natural light. You might be surprised at how much of a difference a small shift can make.

Remember, makeup is personal. These guidelines are a starting point, not a rulebook. Play around with the angle, the intensity, and the products until you find what makes you feel confident. The goal is to enhance your features, not to hide them. A round face is beautiful, and with the right blush placement, you can highlight that beauty in a way that feels fresh and lifted.

posts.title: Office Makeup That Lasts Through Fluorescent Lights: Sheer Base, Soft Eyes, and a Coffee-Proof Lip
posts.excerpt: Fluorescent lights are unforgiving. Here's how to build a sheer base, soft eyes, and a lip that survives coffee, plus a touch-up kit that stays professional.
content: Why Fluorescent Lights Change Everything

You know the feeling. You do your makeup in the warm glow of your bathroom mirror, feel great, then walk into the office and catch your reflection in the elevator. Suddenly your foundation looks chalky, your blush looks patchy, and your lipstick has already started to fade. Fluorescent lights are not your friend. They cast a cool, greenish cast that can make warm tones look off and cool tones look ashy. They also highlight every bit of texture, every dry patch, every crease.

The good news? You can work with fluorescent lights instead of fighting them. The trick is to keep your base sheer and hydrated, choose soft eye colors that don't compete with the lighting, and pick a lip that fades gracefully. And of course, have a touch-up kit that's small enough to stash in your desk drawer without looking like you're moving in.

In this post, I'll walk you through a full office makeup routine that holds up under those harsh lights. I'll share product types, application tips, and a few real-life examples from my own coaching sessions. By the end, you'll have a reliable look that survives coffee, meetings, and the dreaded 3 p.m. fluorescent glare.
Start With Skin Prep That Plays Nice With Fluorescents

Before you even think about foundation, get your skin ready. Fluorescent lights love to highlight dry patches and flakiness, so hydration is your best defense. I always tell my clients to think of their skin as the canvas. If the canvas is rough, the paint won't look smooth.

Start with a gentle cleanser, then apply a hydrating toner or essence. Follow with a lightweight moisturizer that absorbs quickly. If you have oily skin, don't skip moisturizer. Dehydrated skin produces more oil, and that oil can break down makeup faster. Let your moisturizer sit for a minute or two before moving on.

Next, primer. You don't need a heavy silicone primer unless you have large pores you want to blur. A hydrating primer or a smoothing primer with a soft-focus finish works well under fluorescents. Apply it only where you need it: typically the center of your face, avoiding the perimeter where you want a natural finish.

One more thing: wait a few minutes after skincare before applying makeup. This gives everything time to settle and prevents pilling. I know it's tempting to rush, but those few minutes make a big difference in how your makeup wears.
Sheer Base: The Secret to a Natural Look Under Harsh Lights

Heavy foundation is the enemy of fluorescent lighting. The more coverage you pile on, the more likely it is to look cakey or catch the light in unflattering ways. Instead, aim for a sheer, buildable base that evens out your skin tone without masking it.

I prefer a tinted moisturizer or a light-coverage foundation with a natural finish. Apply it with a damp sponge or your fingers, starting in the center of your face and blending outward. Use less product than you think you need. You can always add more, but it's harder to take away.

For areas that need a bit more coverage, like redness around the nose or dark circles, use a small concealer brush and a creamy concealer. Tap it in gently. Avoid heavy powders under the eyes, as they can settle into fine lines and look dry under fluorescents.

Set your base lightly with a finely milled powder only where you get shiny. A light dusting on the T-zone is usually enough. Leave the cheeks and perimeter of your face unpowdered for a natural glow. This also helps your blush blend more seamlessly.
Remember, the goal is to look like you have great skin, not like you're wearing a mask. Sheer layers reflect light more naturally and are more forgiving if you need to touch up later.
Soft Eyes That Don't Compete With Your Base

Under fluorescent lights, heavy eye makeup can look harsh and aging. Soft, blended eyeshadows in neutral or cool-toned shades are your best bet. Think taupe, soft brown, and muted mauve. Avoid anything too warm or too sparkly, as shimmer can catch the light and look distracting.

Start with an eyeshadow primer or a light concealer on your lids. This prevents creasing and helps the shadow last. Then, take a fluffy brush and sweep a light neutral shade all over your lid. Next, use a slightly deeper shade in the crease to add definition. Blend well. The key is seamless transitions.

For a bit of dimension, you can add a tiny amount of matte brown along the lash line instead of a harsh eyeliner. Smudge it with a small brush. This defines your eyes without looking like you tried too hard.

Mascara is essential, but keep it clean. One or two coats on the top lashes, and maybe a light coat on the bottom if you have dark circles. Avoid clumpy formulas. If you want to tightline, use a dark brown pencil instead of black for a softer look.
If you have oily lids, set your primer with a tiny bit of translucent powder before applying shadow. This will help everything stay put through long meetings and that afternoon coffee run.
Cheeks and Brows: The Frame of Your Face

Blush can make or break your look under fluorescents. A cream blush in a soft, natural shade (think dusty rose or peach) blends into the skin and looks more like a natural flush than a powder. Apply it to the apples of your cheeks and blend upward toward your temples. Keep it sheer.
If you prefer powder blush, use a light hand and a fluffy brush. Tap off excess before applying. Build in thin layers. The goal is a soft wash of color, not a stripe.

Brows should look natural, not drawn on. Use a brow pencil or powder that matches your hair color, and fill in sparse areas with short, feathery strokes. Brush through with a spoolie to soften. Avoid harsh, blocky brows, which can look severe under bright lights.

A touch of highlighter on the high points of your cheeks can add a healthy glow, but keep it subtle. A liquid or cream highlighter with a fine shimmer is better than a chunky powder. Apply it before your setting powder if you're using one, or skip powder on those areas.
The Coffee-Proof Lip: How to Choose and Apply
Let's face it: coffee breaks are a ritual. But they can wreck your lipstick. The key is to choose a formula that fades gracefully and apply it in a way that locks in color.

First, decide on the finish. Matte lipsticks last longer but can be drying. Satin or cream finishes are more comfortable but may transfer. A lip stain or tinted balm is a great compromise: it gives a wash of color that fades evenly and keeps lips hydrated.
Prep your lips by exfoliating gently and applying a lip balm. Let it absorb while you do the rest of your makeup. Then, blot off excess balm before applying color.

For a long-lasting look, line and fill your lips with a nude or matching lip liner. This creates a base for the lipstick to cling to. Then apply your lip color with a brush for precision. Blot with a tissue and apply a second layer. This layering technique helps the color last through sips and snacks.

If you're using a traditional lipstick, choose a shade that's close to your natural lip color so that fading is less noticeable. A soft rose, berry, or mauve works well for most skin tones. Avoid very pale or very dark shades, which can look harsh under fluorescents.
And here's a pro tip: carry a tinted lip balm for touch-ups. It adds color and moisture without needing a mirror.
Setting Your Makeup for the Long Haul

Even the best makeup needs a little help to last through an 8-hour day. Setting spray is your friend. Choose one that's hydrating and not too matte. A light mist over your finished makeup helps meld everything together and adds a bit of moisture.
If you have oily skin, you might want to use a mattifying setting spray only on your T-zone. But be careful: too much mattifying product can make your skin look flat under fluorescents.

Another trick is to use a makeup setting powder only where you need it. A light dusting on the T-zone and under the eyes can prevent shine without looking heavy. Avoid baking, which can look cakey under bright lights.

Finally, consider your environment. If you work in a dry office, a hydrating mist throughout the day can refresh your makeup and your skin. If it's humid, you might need a bit more powder. Pay attention to how your makeup wears and adjust.
Touch-Up Kit Ideas That Stay Professional
Your touch-up kit should be small, discreet, and effective. You don't need to bring your whole vanity. Here's what I recommend keeping in your desk drawer or bag.

First, blotting papers. They remove shine without disturbing your makeup. Press, don't rub. Then, a small concealer for any spots that need a quick fix. A cream blush that doubles as a lip color. A tinted lip balm. A travel-sized setting spray. And a small brush or sponge for blending.

Keep everything in a small pouch. Choose products that are multi-use to save space. For example, a cream blush can also be used as an eyeshadow or lip color in a pinch. A tinted lip balm can add color to cheeks as well.
I also like to include a small mirror and a few cotton swabs for fixing smudges. And a tiny bottle of hand sanitizer, because you're touching your face.

Remember, touch-ups should be quick and subtle. You don't want to look like you're reapplying your whole face at your desk. A little blotting, a dab of concealer, a swipe of lip balm, and you're good to go.
Putting It All Together: A Sample Routine
Here's a step-by-step routine you can follow for a reliable office look that lasts.
1. Cleanse and moisturize. Let it absorb.
2. Apply a hydrating primer where needed.
3. Use a tinted moisturizer or light foundation, applied with a damp sponge.
4. Conceal under eyes and any redness.
5. Lightly powder the T-zone.
6. Prime eyelids and apply soft neutral eyeshadow.
7. Smudge matte brown along lash line.
8. Apply mascara.
9. Fill brows with feathery strokes.
10. Apply cream blush to cheeks.
11. Apply lip liner and lip color, blot, and layer.
12. Set with a hydrating setting spray.
This routine should take about 10-15 minutes once you get the hang of it. And it will hold up through fluorescent lights, coffee breaks, and long meetings.
Remember, the best makeup is the kind that makes you feel confident. Adjust these steps to fit your own style and skin needs. And don't forget to smile. That's the best accessory.

I prefer a tinted moisturizer or a light-coverage foundation with a natural finish. Apply it with a damp sponge or your fingers, starting in the center of your face and blending outward. Use less product than you think you need. You can always add more, but it's harder to take away.

For areas that need a bit more coverage, like redness around the nose or dark circles, use a small concealer brush and a creamy concealer. Tap it in gently. Avoid heavy powders under the eyes, as they can settle into fine lines and look dry under fluorescents.

Set your base lightly with a finely milled powder only where you get shiny. A light dusting on the T-zone is usually enough. Leave the cheeks and perimeter of your face unpowdered for a natural glow. This also helps your blush blend more seamlessly.
Remember, the goal is to look like you have great skin, not like you're wearing a mask. Sheer layers reflect light more naturally and are more forgiving if you need to touch up later.

items: Choose a tinted moisturizer or light-coverage foundation.
Apply with a damp sponge for a seamless finish.
Conceal only where needed.
Powder lightly, only on shiny areas.

blocks.text: Sheer base, soft eyes, and a lip that survives coffee. That's the office trifecta.
Soft Eyes That Don't Compete With Your Base

Under fluorescent lights, heavy eye makeup can look harsh and aging. Soft, blended eyeshadows in neutral or cool-toned shades are your best bet. Think taupe, soft brown, and muted mauve. Avoid anything too warm or too sparkly, as shimmer can catch the light and look distracting.

Start with an eyeshadow primer or a light concealer on your lids. This prevents creasing and helps the shadow last. Then, take a fluffy brush and sweep a light neutral shade all over your lid. Next, use a slightly deeper shade in the crease to add definition. Blend well. The key is seamless transitions.

For a bit of dimension, you can add a tiny amount of matte brown along the lash line instead of a harsh eyeliner. Smudge it with a small brush. This defines your eyes without looking like you tried too hard.

Mascara is essential, but keep it clean. One or two coats on the top lashes, and maybe a light coat on the bottom if you have dark circles. Avoid clumpy formulas. If you want to tightline, use a dark brown pencil instead of black for a softer look.
If you have oily lids, set your primer with a tiny bit of translucent powder before applying shadow. This will help everything stay put through long meetings and that afternoon coffee run.

items: Use neutral or cool-toned shadows.
Prime lids to prevent creasing.
Smudge matte brown along lash line instead of harsh liner.
Keep mascara clean and clump-free.

blocks.text: Cheeks and Brows: The Frame of Your Face

Blush can make or break your look under fluorescents. A cream blush in a soft, natural shade (think dusty rose or peach) blends into the skin and looks more like a natural flush than a powder. Apply it to the apples of your cheeks and blend upward toward your temples. Keep it sheer.
If you prefer powder blush, use a light hand and a fluffy brush. Tap off excess before applying. Build in thin layers. The goal is a soft wash of color, not a stripe.

Brows should look natural, not drawn on. Use a brow pencil or powder that matches your hair color, and fill in sparse areas with short, feathery strokes. Brush through with a spoolie to soften. Avoid harsh, blocky brows, which can look severe under bright lights.

A touch of highlighter on the high points of your cheeks can add a healthy glow, but keep it subtle. A liquid or cream highlighter with a fine shimmer is better than a chunky powder. Apply it before your setting powder if you're using one, or skip powder on those areas.

items: Cream blush blends seamlessly and looks natural.
Fill brows with feathery strokes, not blocks.
Use a subtle highlighter for a healthy glow.

blocks.text: The Coffee-Proof Lip: How to Choose and Apply
Let's face it: coffee breaks are a ritual. But they can wreck your lipstick. The key is to choose a formula that fades gracefully and apply it in a way that locks in color.

First, decide on the finish. Matte lipsticks last longer but can be drying. Satin or cream finishes are more comfortable but may transfer. A lip stain or tinted balm is a great compromise: it gives a wash of color that fades evenly and keeps lips hydrated.
Prep your lips by exfoliating gently and applying a lip balm. Let it absorb while you do the rest of your makeup. Then, blot off excess balm before applying color.

For a long-lasting look, line and fill your lips with a nude or matching lip liner. This creates a base for the lipstick to cling to. Then apply your lip color with a brush for precision. Blot with a tissue and apply a second layer. This layering technique helps the color last through sips and snacks.

If you're using a traditional lipstick, choose a shade that's close to your natural lip color so that fading is less noticeable. A soft rose, berry, or mauve works well for most skin tones. Avoid very pale or very dark shades, which can look harsh under fluorescents.
And here's a pro tip: carry a tinted lip balm for touch-ups. It adds color and moisture without needing a mirror.

items: Choose a stain or tinted balm for easy touch-ups.
Line and fill lips with liner for longevity.
Blot and layer lipstick for extra staying power.
Pick a shade close to your natural lip color.

blocks.text: Setting Your Makeup for the Long Haul

Even the best makeup needs a little help to last through an 8-hour day. Setting spray is your friend. Choose one that's hydrating and not too matte. A light mist over your finished makeup helps meld everything together and adds a bit of moisture.
If you have oily skin, you might want to use a mattifying setting spray only on your T-zone. But be careful: too much mattifying product can make your skin look flat under fluorescents.

Another trick is to use a makeup setting powder only where you need it. A light dusting on the T-zone and under the eyes can prevent shine without looking heavy. Avoid baking, which can look cakey under bright lights.

Finally, consider your environment. If you work in a dry office, a hydrating mist throughout the day can refresh your makeup and your skin. If it's humid, you might need a bit more powder. Pay attention to how your makeup wears and adjust.

items: Use a hydrating setting spray.
Powder only where needed.
Adjust for your office environment.

blocks.text: Touch-Up Kit Ideas That Stay Professional
Your touch-up kit should be small, discreet, and effective. You don't need to bring your whole vanity. Here's what I recommend keeping in your desk drawer or bag.

First, blotting papers. They remove shine without disturbing your makeup. Press, don't rub. Then, a small concealer for any spots that need a quick fix. A cream blush that doubles as a lip color. A tinted lip balm. A travel-sized setting spray. And a small brush or sponge for blending.

Keep everything in a small pouch. Choose products that are multi-use to save space. For example, a cream blush can also be used as an eyeshadow or lip color in a pinch. A tinted lip balm can add color to cheeks as well.
I also like to include a small mirror and a few cotton swabs for fixing smudges. And a tiny bottle of hand sanitizer, because you're touching your face.

Remember, touch-ups should be quick and subtle. You don't want to look like you're reapplying your whole face at your desk. A little blotting, a dab of concealer, a swipe of lip balm, and you're good to go.

items: Blotting papers
Small concealer
Cream blush (multi-use)
Tinted lip balm
Travel setting spray
Cotton swabs

blocks.text: Putting It All Together: A Sample Routine
Here's a step-by-step routine you can follow for a reliable office look that lasts.
1. Cleanse and moisturize. Let it absorb.
2. Apply a hydrating primer where needed.
3. Use a tinted moisturizer or light foundation, applied with a damp sponge.
4. Conceal under eyes and any redness.
5. Lightly powder the T-zone.
6. Prime eyelids and apply soft neutral eyeshadow.
7. Smudge matte brown along lash line.
8. Apply mascara.
9. Fill brows with feathery strokes.
10. Apply cream blush to cheeks.
11. Apply lip liner and lip color, blot, and layer.
12. Set with a hydrating setting spray.
This routine should take about 10-15 minutes once you get the hang of it. And it will hold up through fluorescent lights, coffee breaks, and long meetings.
Remember, the best makeup is the kind that makes you feel confident. Adjust these steps to fit your own style and skin needs. And don't forget to smile. That's the best accessory.

items: Prep skin well.
Keep base sheer.
Soft eyes, defined brows.
Cream blush for a natural flush.
Coffee-proof lip with liner and layering.

posts.title: How to Photograph Your Face So AI Makeup Tools Read You Correctly
posts.excerpt: Your selfie is the input. If the lighting, angle, or filter is off, the AI makeup try-on will be off too. Here's how to take a clean photo that gives you useful results, plus free tools to practice.
content: Why Your Selfie Is the Whole Ballgame

I've watched people try virtual makeup for years, and the same thing happens almost every time. Someone uploads a photo with a window blazing behind them, the app puts blush on their forehead, and they blame the tool. But the tool didn't fail. The photo did.

AI makeup tools work by finding your facial landmarks first: the corners of your eyes, the bridge of your nose, the edges of your lips. If those points are wrong, everything that follows is wrong. Lighting, angle, hair, and filters all change what the AI sees. Fix the photo and you fix the result.
Think of it like this: a makeup artist can't match your foundation in a dark club. An AI can't either. Give it a clean, evenly lit, front-facing shot and it can actually do its job.
Lighting: Soft, Even, and In Front of You

The best light for any face analysis is soft and even. Stand facing a window during the day. Not with the window behind you. Facing it. That gives you diffused light across your whole face with no harsh shadows.

If you don't have good natural light, use a ring light or a lamp with a diffuser. Put it slightly above eye level and directly in front. Avoid overhead lights that cast shadows under your eyes and nose. Those shadows can confuse landmark detection and make contour or blush placement look off.

Also watch for mixed color temperatures. A warm lamp on one side and cool window light on the other will tint your skin differently on each side. The AI may read that as uneven tone and adjust makeup in ways you didn't intend. Turn off the lamp or close the curtain. One light source is easier for both you and the algorithm.
Angle: Straight On, Camera at Eye Level

The classic selfie angle, chin down and camera high, is great for Instagram. It's terrible for AI makeup analysis. That angle distorts proportions, hides your jawline, and makes your forehead look larger. The AI then places contour and highlight based on a face shape you don't actually have.
For analysis and try-on, hold the camera at eye level. Look straight into the lens. Keep your head level, not tilted. Your whole face should be visible from hairline to chin, and from ear to ear.

A tripod or a stack of books helps. Prop your phone, set a timer, and step back. You want a little space between you and the camera so the lens doesn't widen your nose. Most phone front cameras are wide angle, and up close they exaggerate the center of your face. Arm's length or a bit more is usually right.
Hair Off the Face and a Clean Background

Hair is the number one thing I see blocking good AI reads. A few strands across the cheek can look like a shadow or a contour line. Bangs covering your forehead hide the top landmarks. Tie your hair back, or at least pin it away from your cheeks and forehead.

Background matters less, but a plain wall helps. A busy background with strong patterns or bright objects can pull the AI's attention or create edge artifacts around your face. Stand a few feet from a plain wall. Avoid standing right against it so you don't cast a shadow.

If you wear glasses, take them off for the photo unless you're specifically testing eye makeup with glasses. Frames can block eye corners and confuse eye makeup placement. Same goes for heavy jewelry near the face.
No Heavy Filters Before Analysis or Try-On

This is the big one. Beauty filters smooth skin, change eye size, slim the jaw, and alter skin tone. If you upload a filtered photo, the AI is analyzing a face that isn't yours. The makeup placement will be based on edited features. Then when you try the look in real life, it won't match.

Turn off all filters in your camera app. That includes the automatic ones some phones apply without telling you. Check your settings. If your photo looks smoother than what you see in the mirror, it's filtered.

You also want a neutral expression. Don't smile too wide or scrunch your eyes. A relaxed, closed-mouth expression keeps your features in their natural position. That gives the AI the most accurate landmarks to work from.

If you've been getting weird results and you're not sure why, start with a clean photo. There's a free guide on [first photo setup for face tools](https://rizzassistgo.com/blog/first-photo-setup-face-tools/) that walks through the basics step by step. It's a good sanity check before you blame the app.
Eye and Face Landmark Accuracy: Why Small Things Matter

Eye makeup is where bad photos show up fastest. If the AI misreads your eye corners, winged liner will point the wrong way. If it misreads your lid space, shadow will sit too high or too low. That's why eye-level, straight-on shots matter so much.
You also want your eyes open and looking at the camera. Not down at your phone screen. Looking down changes the shape of your lid and can make the AI place crease color in the wrong spot.

For a deeper walkthrough on getting eye and face landmarks right, there's a [photo setup guide for face and eye AI tools](https://rizzassistgo.com/blog/photo-setup-guide-face-eye-ai-tools/) that covers distance, focus, and expression. It's worth a read if you plan to test eye looks often.
One more tip: clean your lens. A smudged phone camera adds haze and softens edges. The AI has less to work with. A quick wipe with a microfiber cloth makes a real difference.
A Simple Photo Setup You Can Repeat
Here's a routine I give students. It takes two minutes and saves a lot of frustration.

Step one: find a spot facing a window or a soft lamp. Step two: tie your hair back and take off glasses. Step three: prop your phone at eye level, set a timer, and step back to arm's length. Step four: turn off all filters, relax your face, and take three shots. Step five: pick the one where your whole face is evenly lit and in focus.
Save that photo. Use it as your baseline for every AI makeup test. When you change your hair or lighting, take a new baseline. Consistency is what makes your results comparable.
Practice With a Free Face Shape Tool

Once you have a clean front-facing photo, a good way to check that the AI is reading you correctly is to run it through a simple analysis tool. The [face shape detector](https://rizzassistgo.com/face-shape-detector/) on Rizz Assist is free and gives you a quick read on your face shape. If the result matches what you know about your face, your photo is probably clean. If it's way off, your lighting or angle needs work.

This is also a low-pressure way to practice your photo setup. You're not testing a full makeup look. You're just checking that the input is good. Once the face shape read looks right, you can move on to try-on with confidence.
Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
Here are the issues I see most often, and the fixes.
Backlighting: your face is dark and the window is bright. Fix: turn around and face the window.
Tilted head: the AI reads a different jawline. Fix: level your chin and look straight ahead.
Hair across the cheek: reads as a shadow. Fix: pin it back.
Beauty filter: changes your features. Fix: turn it off in camera settings.
Too close to the lens: exaggerates your nose and center face. Fix: step back and use a timer.
Looking down at the screen: changes your eye shape. Fix: look at the lens, not the preview.
Putting It All Together

AI makeup tools are only as good as the photo you feed them. Soft even light, a straight-on angle at eye level, hair off your face, and no filters will get you results that actually translate to real life. It's not about taking a prettier selfie. It's about taking an honest one.

Take five minutes to set up your baseline photo today. Then test one look. If it lands where you expect, you know your input is solid. If it doesn't, go back to the checklist. Nine times out of ten, the fix is in the photo, not the tool.

posts.title: Lip Liner That Shapes Without Looking Drawn On
posts.excerpt: Lip liner doesn't have to look like a stencil. Learn how to shape your cupid's bow, corners, and fill for thin, full, or uneven lips with shade pairing tips that keep it soft and natural.
content: Why Lip Liner Gets a Bad Rep

You've seen it: the ring of dark liner around a lighter lip, like a lipstick halo from 1995. That's not lip liner's fault. That's a technique problem. When liner is used to create a hard outline, it looks drawn on. When it's used to shape and blend, it looks like your lips but better.

The goal is definition, not demarcation. Think of liner as a soft shadow at the edges, not a fence. Your lips should look shaped, not traced. That means choosing the right shade, applying with a light hand, and blending like you mean it.
Pick the Right Shade (Hint: It's Not Always Your Lipstick)

The biggest mistake is matching liner to your lipstick. That can work, but it often creates a flat, opaque edge. Instead, match your liner to your lips. Not your lipstick, not your outfit, your lips. That means looking at your natural lip color, not the color you wish you had.

For most people, the perfect liner is one to two shades deeper than your natural lip tone, with the same undertone. If your lips are cool pink, don't grab a warm terracotta. If they're warm peach, skip the mauve. Swatch on your fingertip, not your hand, because fingertip color is closer to lip color.
The Cupid's Bow: Soften, Don't Sharpen

The cupid's bow is where liner goes wrong fastest. A sharp, pointed peak looks drawn on, especially in daylight. The fix is to soften the peak, not define it. Start at the very center of your top lip and draw two short, angled strokes downward, following the natural dip. Don't connect them at the top. Leave a tiny gap.

Then, using a small brush or your fingertip, press and roll the liner upward to blur the edges. The goal is a soft peak that mimics the natural shadow of your lip, not a graphic V. If your bow is uneven, don't try to fix it with liner alone. Use a concealer brush to clean up the smaller side, then line both sides to match the fuller side.
The Corners: Define Without Extending

The corners of your mouth are where liner can make you look like you're scowling or like you've had work done. The trick is to define the corner without extending past it. Place the tip of the liner right at the corner, then draw a tiny stroke outward and slightly down, following the natural crease. That's it. One millimeter, not five.

If your lips turn down naturally, don't try to draw them up. Instead, use a touch of concealer at the very corner to lift the appearance, then line only the bottom edge of the corner. This keeps the shape soft and prevents that drawn-on look.
Filling: The Secret to a Seamless Look

Most people only line the edges, but filling the entire lip with liner is what makes it last and look natural. It creates a base that grips lipstick and prevents feathering. But you don't want to color outside the lines. Fill only the inner portion of your lips, staying away from the very edge you just lined.

Use the side of the pencil, not the tip, and fill in small circular motions. Then blend everything together with a lip brush or your finger. The liner should melt into your lips, not sit on top. If you're using a lipstick, apply it now, pressing it into the liner rather than swiping it on.
Thin Lips: How to Add Volume Without Overlining

Overlining thin lips is a trap. It looks obvious and feels uncomfortable. Instead, focus on enhancing what you have. Start by lining just outside your natural lip line, but only at the center of your top and bottom lip. That adds a subtle plumpness without looking drawn on.

Then, fill the rest of your lips with liner, and apply a lipstick that's one shade lighter than your liner in the center. This creates an optical illusion of fullness. Avoid dark mattes, which can make lips look smaller. Go for satin or glossy finishes that reflect light.
Full Lips: Shape Without Shrinking

Full lips are a gift, but they can look messy with liner if you're not careful. The goal is to define the shape without making them look smaller. Use a liner that's an exact match to your lip color, and line right on the natural edge. Don't go inside the line, that shrinks the lip.

posts.title: Clean Girl Makeup That Doesn’t Look Unfinished
posts.excerpt: A skin-first routine with brow gel, cream blush, mascara, and lip oil. Tips for dry and oily skin so you look polished, not half-done.
content: Why Clean Girl Makeup Can Look Unfinished

You know the look: fresh skin, fluffy brows, a hint of blush, and a glossy lip. It’s supposed to feel effortless. But sometimes it just feels… incomplete. Like you forgot a step or ran out the door before finishing. The difference between “clean girl” and “clean but unfinished” comes down to intention. Every product has a job, and placement matters more than quantity.

I’ve coached this look on clients from dry to oily, and the biggest mistake is treating it like a no-makeup makeup free-for-all. Clean girl makeup still needs structure. You’re building a base that looks like skin, then adding just enough definition to frame your face. When something looks off, it’s usually because one area is too flat or too heavy. The fix is rarely more product. It’s better placement and prep.
Start With Skin Prep for Your Skin Type

Clean girl makeup lives or dies on skin. If your base looks like a mask, the whole look reads as unfinished because it doesn’t match the rest of your face. Prep is where you win. For dry skin, think hydration without heaviness. For oily skin, think balance without stripping.

Dry skin: layer a hydrating toner or essence, then a moisturizer with ceramides or glycerin. Let it sink in for a minute. If you have flaky patches, gently press a tiny bit of facial oil on those spots only. Wait five minutes before makeup. That wait matters. It keeps your foundation from sliding or clinging to dry bits.

Oily skin: use a lightweight gel moisturizer and a mattifying primer only where you get shiny, like the T-zone. Don’t mattify your whole face. You want a natural finish, not flat. A blurring primer on the center of the face helps makeup stay put without looking powdery. Skip heavy creams. They’ll break down your base by lunch.

Both skin types: sunscreen is non-negotiable. Choose one that works with your makeup. For dry skin, a hydrating chemical sunscreen. For oily skin, a gel or fluid formula. Let it set for a few minutes before you go in with base.
Base That Looks Like Skin, Not Foundation

The goal is evening out tone, not covering your face. Use a sheer to medium coverage foundation or a tinted moisturizer. Apply it with a damp sponge or your fingers, starting in the center of your face and blending outward. Sheer it out at the edges so there’s no line. If you need more coverage, add a tiny dot of concealer only where you need it: under the eyes, around the nose, or on a spot.

For dry skin, avoid powder entirely except for a light dusting under the eyes if you need it. A cream or liquid formula will sit better. For oily skin, set only the areas that get shiny with a finely milled powder. Use a small fluffy brush and press, don’t sweep. Sweeping kicks up texture and makes everything look patchy.

One trick that keeps clean girl makeup looking finished: use a hydrating setting spray after base. It melts everything together and takes away any powdery look. For oily skin, choose a mattifying setting spray instead. Mist, then press with clean hands.
Brow Gel: The Difference Between Fluffy and Messy

Brow gel is the backbone of clean girl makeup. It gives you that feathery, lifted look. But if you just swipe and go, you can end up with brows that look wild or crunchy. The key is to use the right amount and shape them as you go.

Start by brushing your brows up and over with a spoolie. Then take a tinted or clear brow gel. Wipe off excess on the edge of the tube. Apply in short upward strokes, following the direction of hair growth. For the front of the brow, brush the hairs straight up. For the tail, brush them outward. If you have sparse spots, use a fine-tipped brow pen to draw in individual hairs before the gel. That keeps it looking natural, not drawn on.

For dry skin, a clear gel with a bit of glycerin works well because it adds a slight sheen. For oily skin, choose a gel with stronger hold, and avoid putting gel on your brow bone where it can make your whole face look shiny. If your brows are very curly or coarse, a tinted gel with fibers can help fill and hold at the same time.
Cream Blush: Placement Makes It Look Finished

Cream blush is perfect for clean girl makeup because it melts into skin and looks like a natural flush. But if you dot it on and don’t blend, it can look like two circles. Or worse, it can sit on top of your base and emphasize texture.

The trick is to apply cream blush with your fingers or a damp sponge, and blend it out immediately. Smile to find the apples of your cheeks, then place a small amount and blend up toward your temples. For a lifted look, place a tiny bit higher, near the top of your cheekbone, and blend. That’s especially flattering if you have a round face or want a more sculpted effect.

For dry skin, cream blush is your best friend. It adds hydration and a dewy finish. For oily skin, cream blush can slide, so set it with a tiny bit of translucent powder or a matching powder blush on top. That locks it in without losing the glow. If you have textured cheeks, avoid putting blush right on the texture. Place it slightly above or below.
Mascara: Define Without Clumps
Mascara is where clean girl makeup can go wrong fast. Too much and it looks heavy. Too little and your eyes disappear. The goal is definition: darker, slightly longer lashes that still look soft.

Start by curling your lashes. That opens your eyes more than mascara alone. Then take a lengthening or separating mascara. Wipe the wand on the edge of the tube to remove excess. Apply from root to tip in a zigzag motion, focusing on the roots. One coat is usually enough for clean girl. If you want more, add a second coat only on the tips. Avoid pumping the wand. It pushes air into the tube and dries out the formula, which leads to clumps.

For dry skin, a tubing mascara is great because it doesn’t flake and removes easily. For oily skin, choose a waterproof or smudge-proof formula, especially if your eyelids get oily. But keep it light. Heavy mascara fights the clean girl vibe. If you have sparse lashes, use a lash primer first. It adds volume without weight.
Lip Oil: Hydration That Looks Polished

Lip oil gives that glossy, juicy look that’s central to clean girl makeup. But if your lips are dry or the oil wears off unevenly, it can look messy. Prep is key. Exfoliate your lips gently once or twice a week with a damp washcloth or a sugar scrub. Then apply a hydrating lip balm and let it sink in while you do the rest of your makeup.

When you’re ready, blot off excess balm and apply lip oil. Start in the center and blend outward. For a hint of color, choose a tinted lip oil. If you have dry skin, a lip oil with jojoba or squalane will feel comfortable and not sticky. For oily skin, choose a lighter formula that won’t slide around. If you’re prone to lip lines, avoid putting oil right in the center of your lower lip. Place it slightly off-center and blend.
To keep the look finished, carry the lip oil with you and reapply after eating or drinking. A quick swipe and blend with your finger keeps it looking intentional.
Putting It All Together: A 10-Minute Routine

Here’s a simple order that keeps clean girl makeup looking polished, not unfinished. Prep your skin based on your type. Apply sunscreen. Then base: sheer foundation or tinted moisturizer, concealer only where needed. Set only oily zones if you’re oily. Move to brows: brush up, fill sparse spots, set with gel. Then cream blush: blend well. Mascara: one light coat. Lip oil: prep and apply. Finish with setting spray if you want everything to melt together.

The whole thing should take about ten minutes once you’ve practiced. The key is to keep each step light. If something looks off, don’t add more. Instead, blend more or remove a bit. Clean girl makeup is about enhancing what you have, not covering it up. When you focus on skin, brows, blush, mascara, and lips, you get a look that feels fresh and finished at the same time.

posts.title: Warm, Cool, or Neutral Foundation: How to Find Your Undertone Without the Orange Cast
posts.excerpt: Tired of foundation that turns orange by lunch? Learn why the vein test can mislead you, how to swatch on your jawline the right way, and how to fix a shade that looked fine indoors.
content: Why Your Foundation Turns Orange (And It’s Not Always the Formula)

You’ve seen it: you apply foundation in the morning, it looks seamless, and by 2 p.m. your face is a shade of tangerine that doesn’t match your neck. Before you blame the brand, know this: the orange cast usually comes from a mismatch in undertone, not from the foundation itself oxidizing. Oxidation happens, sure, but most of the time it’s the wrong undertone reacting with your skin’s natural oils and the environment.

Undertone is the subtle hue beneath your skin’s surface. It’s different from overtone, which is the surface color you see (fair, light, medium, deep). You can have a fair overtone with a warm undertone, or a deep overtone with a cool undertone. When you pick a foundation with the wrong undertone, it can look okay for a few minutes, but as it mixes with your skin’s natural chemistry, the color shifts. Warm foundations on cool skin can turn peachy or orange. Cool foundations on warm skin can turn ashy or gray.

The fix isn’t to keep buying new foundations. It’s to learn how to identify your undertone accurately and then choose a foundation that matches. In this post, I’ll walk you through the limits of the vein test, how to swatch on your jawline properly, and what to do if you’ve already got a foundation that looked fine indoors but turns orange outside.
The Vein Test: What It Can and Can’t Tell You

The vein test is the most common undertone trick: look at the veins on your wrist. If they appear blue or purple, you’re cool. If they look green, you’re warm. If you see a mix, you’re neutral. It’s a good starting point, but it’s not gospel. I’ve seen plenty of people with warm undertones whose veins look blue, and cool undertones with green-looking veins. Why? Because vein color depends on how light scatters through your skin, not just on your undertone. Skin thickness, hydration, and even the lighting in the room can change what you see.

Another limitation: the vein test only looks at one small area. Your face might have different undertones than your wrist.
